solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Lug instrument and books round room

blocks.note: OT is the Old Testament, a collection of books
a round shape is the letter O
room to manoeuvre is scope

explanation.surface: Someone hauls a musical instrument and a pile of books around a room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lug' looks like a verb meaning carry, but it is informal British slang for the ear, so the definition is an ear instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: An otoscope is the medical device a doctor uses to look inside the ear canal.

clue.text: Birds squawk

blocks.note: first meaning: game birds shot on British moors; the plural is the same as the singular
second meaning: to complain loudly

explanation.surface: A flock of birds makes a racket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'squawk' looks like the noise the birds make, but here it means to complain, a separate sense of the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: The game bird name has an identical plural, and as a verb the word means grumble or protest.

clue.text: Man on board vessel housing wife

indicators.note: to house something is to give it a home inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: a pan is a cooking vessel
W is the standard abbreviation for wife

explanation.surface: A sailor aboard ship who has his wife living with him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man on board' suggests a sailor and 'vessel' a ship, but the board is a chessboard and the vessel a pan.
explanation.definitionFit: Chess pieces are called men, and the pawn is the humblest piece on the chessboard.

clue.text: Cereal stuck in my beard

indicators.note: something stuck in another thing is lodged inside it

blocks.note: 'my!' and 'gee!' are both exclamations of surprise
oats are a cereal crop

explanation.surface: Someone complains that breakfast cereal has got caught in their beard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'my' reads as a possessive but is the exclamation, swapped for another exclamation of surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: A goatee is a small pointed tuft of facial hair on the chin, one style of beard.

clue.text: Canine abdomen sadly containing tip of finger

indicators.note: something going sadly is going wrong, so the letters fall out of order
a tip is an end, so only one end letter of the word is kept
to contain is to hold within, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
the tip at the far end of the word

explanation.surface: A dog with a sore belly, sadly holding its paw tip.
explanation.walkthrough: The tip here is the end of the word rather than its start, so it is the last letter of finger that goes inside the rearranged abdomen.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dobermann is a breed of dog, so it is a canine; the word works as a noun here.

clue.text: Success upset sweet kid

indicators.note: to upset is to overturn, which in a down clue turns the letters upside down

blocks.note: a win is a success
pud is British slang for pudding, a sweet or dessert

explanation.surface: A child is upset after doing well, perhaps a dear little kid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sweet kid' looks like a charming child, but kid is the verb to tease and sweet is the dessert course.
explanation.definitionFit: To wind someone up is British slang for teasing or provoking them, just as kidding is.

clue.text: Count is really disheartened

indicators.note: losing heart means losing the centre, so the middle letters are removed

blocks.note: taken as written, before its centre is dropped

explanation.surface: A nobleman, a count, is truly downhearted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Count' looks like a nobleman, but it is the verb in 'count on'. The heart of really is its middle two letters AL.
explanation.definitionFit: To count on someone is to depend on them, so the verb is a synonym for trust or depend.

clue.text: Violent storm to bother sheltering Navy

indicators.note: to shelter something is to keep it inside under cover

blocks.note: taken as written
ado is fuss or bother
RN is the Royal Navy

explanation.surface: A violent storm makes trouble for the fleet, which must take shelter.
explanation.walkthrough: Royal Navy is abbreviated RN, the British fleet.
explanation.definitionFit: A tornado is a destructive rotating column of wind, an extreme kind of storm.

clue.text: Volunteer work, popular introduction to employment

indicators.note: an introduction comes at the start, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: op is short for opus, a work
something popular is in
its opening letter

explanation.surface: Unpaid charity work is a popular way to get into a job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Volunteer work' reads as one phrase about charity, but Volunteer is a verb on its own: to offer up a view unasked.
explanation.definitionFit: To opine is to give an opinion, and volunteering a view means offering it freely.

clue.text: Slight prod necessary at first

indicators.note: what comes at first is the opening, so only the initial letter is kept

blocks.note: a spur is a prod to a horse
its opening letter

explanation.surface: A gentle nudge is needed to get started.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slight' reads as an adjective meaning small, but it is the verb to snub.
explanation.definitionFit: To slight someone is to treat them with disdain, and to spurn is to reject them scornfully.

clue.text: University dons stayed drunk for 24 hours

indicators.note: a drunk person is unsteady and muddled, so the letters stagger into a new order
to don is to put on clothing, so one piece wraps itself around the other

blocks.note: U is the abbreviation for university
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: College lecturers stayed drunk for a whole day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dons' looks like the noun for university teachers, but it is the verb meaning puts on: the rearranged letters put on the U.
explanation.definitionFit: Any weekday lasts a full day of twenty-four hours, so this one is an example of the definition.

clue.text: Clobber whoever spoilt latter half of film

indicators.note: something spoilt is damaged and messed up, so the letters are jumbled
keeping only the latter half means the front half is cut away

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
taken as written, before its first two letters go

explanation.surface: A threat to beat up anyone who gave away the ending of a movie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clobber' can be a British noun for clothes or gear, but here it is the verb to defeat heavily.
explanation.definitionFit: To clobber an opponent is to beat them soundly, which is to crush or overpower them completely.

clue.text: Effete old chap seized by desire

indicators.note: something seized is gripped and held, so it sits inside the other piece

blocks.note: a wish is a desire
O is the abbreviation for old
a chap is a man

explanation.surface: A foppish elderly gentleman is overcome with longing.
explanation.walkthrough: The O and the chap together go inside the desire.
explanation.definitionFit: Effete describes a man seen as weak and unmanly, which this old-fashioned and pejorative adjective also conveys.

clue.text: Old man left mate

blocks.note: one's old man is one's father, or pa
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: An elderly man abandoned his partner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left' looks like the past tense of leave, but it is the direction, abbreviated; 'Old man' is informal for father.
explanation.definitionFit: Mate is British and Australian slang for a friend, and a pal is likewise a close friend.

clue.text: Operating theatre’s closing for benefit of patients?

definitions.text: Operating theatre’s closing for benefit of patients?

blocks.clueFragment: Operating theatre’s closing for benefit of patients?
blocks.note: surface reading: a hospital theatre is shutting down, supposedly for the patients' good
setter's reading: the thread a surgeon uses in theatre to tie off and close a blood vessel

explanation.surface: A hospital announces its operating theatre is shutting, claiming it helps the patients.
explanation.walkthrough: 'closing' reads as a shutdown of the theatre, but it is the noun for a thing that closes, the tie a surgeon applies during an operation.
explanation.definitionFit: Surgeons use this thread or cord to tie off blood vessels and stop bleeding during operations.

clue.text: Slippery character returned three letters from Middle East

indicators.note: taking a run of letters from a phrase means the word sits inside the text
something returned goes back the way it came, so the letters read backwards

blocks.note: the three letters straddling the two words

explanation.surface: A shifty person came back with three letters from the Middle East.
explanation.walkthrough: 'three letters from Middle East' suggests an abbreviation like ME, but it means three consecutive letters taken from the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: An eel is a famously slimy fish, and a slippery character is someone hard to pin down, the same image.

clue.text: Fat peer regularly seen in pantry

indicators.note: doing something regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

blocks.note: lard is pig fat
its second and fourth letters

explanation.surface: An overweight lord is often spotted in the food cupboard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'peer' could be the verb to look, but here it is only a source of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A larder is a cool room or cupboard for storing food, so it is a synonym of the other storeroom word.

clue.text: Revolting rum in tiny mug

indicators.note: rum is British slang for odd or strange, so the letters are put in a peculiar order
one thing in another sits inside it

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone finds it disgusting that rum is served in a tiny cup.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rum' wants to be the drink, but it is the adjective meaning odd, applied to the words that follow it, which then go inside the mug. 'Revolting' is not disgusting but rising up.
explanation.definitionFit: Revolting here means rebelling against authority, as sailors do when they rise against their officers.

clue.text: Canter about in daze

indicators.note: about suggests moving around, so the letters are turned into a different order

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A horse goes around at a gentle pace in a dreamy state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' joins the wordplay to the definition, so the result is what you are in when dazed.
explanation.definitionFit: A trance is a half-conscious dreamlike state, much like being stunned or dazed.

clue.text: Setter’s initially nervous after dog attack

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter is kept
following something places it later in the sequence of letters

blocks.note: the setter refers to themself as I, so the setter's, or setter is, gives I'M
a pug is a breed of small dog
its opening letter

explanation.surface: The crossword compiler admits to being jittery after being bitten by a dog.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters often call themselves 'I' or 'me'; here the apostrophe-s turns that into I'M.
explanation.definitionFit: To impugn a claim or someone's character is to challenge or criticise it, a verbal attack.

clue.text: Some clever Andalusians open gallery

indicators.note: taking only some of the text means part of the words is used, a run within them

blocks.note: spans the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Smart people from southern Spain open an art gallery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'open' looks like a verb about the Andalusians launching a gallery, but it is an adjective in the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A veranda is a roofed platform along the outside of a house, open at the sides like a gallery.

clue.text: Five naked gents let off steam

indicators.note: naked means stripped of covering, so the outer letters are removed and the middle stays

blocks.note: V is the Roman numeral for five
its inner letters without the outer pair

explanation.surface: Five men with no clothes on blow off steam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'naked' is used for removing the first and last letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To vent anger or feelings is to release them, an idiom for letting off steam.

clue.text: Roughly position head for doctor

blocks.note: ca is short for circa, Latin for roughly or about
to position something is to put it

explanation.surface: Someone has a rough go at locating the head of a medical team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head for doctor' suggests a chief medic, but it means the doctor's word for head: caput is the anatomical Latin term.
explanation.definitionFit: Anatomists and physicians use the Latin word for the head of the body, or a head-like part of an organ.

clue.text: Bloke is quiet after tea

indicators.note: following something places it later in the sequence of letters

blocks.note: cha is a British slang word for tea
p is piano, the musical direction for quiet

explanation.surface: A man falls silent once he has had his cup of tea.
explanation.walkthrough: In musical notation p, piano, means play quietly.
explanation.definitionFit: Bloke and chap are both informal British words for a man or fellow.

clue.text: Previously called with extremely dubious demands

indicators.note: extremely refers to the extremes, so just the outer letters are kept

blocks.note: née marks a woman's maiden name, what she was called before
its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Someone who once phoned up with highly questionable requests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'called' looks like phoned, but 'Previously called' is the formal marker for a former name.
explanation.definitionFit: Demands as a plural noun are requirements, and needs are things that are required.

clue.text: Fury after vacuous clerical mistake

indicators.note: vacuous means empty, so the inside is cleared out and only the outer letters remain
following something places it later in the sequence of letters

blocks.note: its first and last letters
fury is great anger

explanation.surface: Rage follows a thoughtless office error.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clerical mistake' looks like the definition, but only 'mistake' is; clangers are a British word for embarrassing blunders.
explanation.definitionFit: A clanger is British slang for a conspicuous blunder, so it means an error.
